1058.title: Thomas Becket (29 December)
1058.hook: the archbishop killed in his own cathedral
1058.howItsDone: Catholics may keep Saint Thomas Becket's memorial on 29 December, inside the Christmas octave, and in England his feast is kept with special honor; pilgrims still visit the place of his martyrdom in Canterbury Cathedral.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John the Evangelist, the disciple whom Jesus loved, resting his head on Jesus at supper. Your line was the beloved disciple. Did you let yourself be held, even for a minute? Day one thousand fifty-eight.

Late afternoon, winter, Canterbury. The monks are singing the evening office when armed knights come in from the cloister, looking for the archbishop. His monks panic and run to bolt the doors behind him. He stops them. A visiting cleric named Edward Grim was there, and he tells us what the archbishop said: a church is not to be made into a castle. Leave the doors open. A few minutes later, Thomas Becket was dead on the floor of his own cathedral. So how did the king's friend end up there?
screen: `EVENING PRAYER AT CANTERBURY.` → `KNIGHTS IN THE CLOISTER.` → `LEAVE THE DOORS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Thomas started as the king's man. He was chancellor to King Henry the Second, his friend, his right hand, famous for fine clothes and a big household. When the archbishop of Canterbury died, Henry pushed to have Thomas put in the job, expecting a friend at the head of the English Church. What he got was a different man. The old accounts say Thomas began to live simply under his robes and to pray long hours. And he started saying no to the king, above all over whether clergy accused of crimes would be tried in the king's courts or the Church's. The quarrel grew bitter. Thomas fled into exile in France, and stayed away a long time. A fragile peace brought him home. Then Henry, angry at news from Canterbury, said something in his hall. Nobody agrees on the exact words; the line you may have heard about a troublesome priest is a later retelling. But some knights heard it as permission and rode for the cathedral. Grim, who tried to shield the archbishop and was wounded himself, says Thomas went to his death commending himself and the Church to God. Here's what makes his feast more than a murder story. Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep." The accounts don't make him gentle; he could be proud and stubborn. And yet at the end he stood still and kept the door open. Chroniclers say the king himself later came to the tomb in penance, and pilgrims kept coming to Canterbury long after him.
screen: `THE KING'S FRIEND AND CHANCELLOR.` · `THE ARCHBISHOP WHO SAID NO.` · `KILLED IN HIS OWN CATHEDRAL.` · `THE GOOD SHEPHERD GIVETH HIS LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for church leaders. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who carries responsibility for a community: a bishop, a pastor, a parish priest, a youth minister, the person who runs your local shelter or your kid's school. Picture them at the end of a long day, tired, facing a decision with no easy answer. If you pray, you can ask that they have courage when they need to say no, and humility when they don't. If you don't pray, simply hold them in your attention, and wish them a clear head. The bell holds the time.
Thomas Becket. The king's friend who became archbishop of Canterbury, stood against the king, and was killed in his own cathedral with the doors left open. Today's word.
Your line: killed in the cathedral. Today, when you walk through a door, let it remind you of the archbishop who wouldn't let his be bolted. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

1059.title: Sylvester (31 December)
1059.hook: the pope of Constantine's time, kept on New Year's Eve
1059.howItsDone: Catholics may keep Saint Sylvester's memorial on 31 December; in some parishes the year ends with Mass or with a hymn of thanksgiving, the Te Deum, sung on the evening of the last day of the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas Becket, the archbishop who told his monks to leave the doors open. Your line was killed in the cathedral. Did you hold a church leader in your prayer or your attention? Day one thousand fifty-nine.

Why would a New Year's party be named after a pope? In Vienna or Berlin, ask what the night of 31 December is called and you may hear a name instead of a date: Silvester. In Warsaw, Sylwester. Fireworks, countdowns, glasses raised at midnight, and the whole night carries a saint's name. He was a pope, and his feast happens to fall on the last day of the calendar year. Today, the man whose name ends the year.
screen: `A PARTY NAMED FOR A POPE?` → `SILVESTER, SYLWESTER.` → `WHO WAS SYLVESTER?`

segments.voice: Sylvester was bishop of Rome in the time of the emperor Constantine, the years when persecution gave way to imperial favor. Before, Christians could lose their property or their lives for gathering to worship. Now an emperor was building churches. For a pope in that moment, everything was changing. Here's the honest part: we know surprisingly little for certain about Sylvester himself. The old book of the popes, the Liber Pontificalis, lists churches built and gifts given in his time. When the bishops gathered at Nicaea to answer the question of who Christ is, the usual account is that Sylvester didn't travel there himself, but sent representatives. And where the facts ran thin, stories grew. A later legend says Sylvester cured Constantine of a disease and baptized him in Rome. The older histories tell it differently, with the emperor baptized near the end of his life, far from Rome. So the Church remembers a pope partly hidden behind his own legends. Maybe that's fitting for a man kept on New Year's Eve. A year can look like that from its last night: a few moments stay clear, and the rest blurs. A psalm in the Douay-Rheims says to God, "Thou shalt bless the crown of the year of thy goodness." The crown of the year: the whole circle of it, the clear days and the blurry ones, held up and blessed. Sylvester's feast puts a saint at the very edge of the calendar, and some Catholics read that as a sign that even the last night of the year belongs to God.
screen: `THE POPE OF CONSTANTINE'S TIME.` · `LITTLE KNOWN FOR CERTAIN.` · `LEGENDS FILL THE GAPS.` · `THE CROWN OF THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for the year. Settle, and breathe. Let this year go by like pages turning, without stopping to fix anything. A morning you remember. A person who showed up. Something that went wrong and turned out survivable. Something small that you'd forgotten until now. When one comes back, stay with it for a breath and say thank you, inside. If you pray, you can offer the whole year back to God, the clear parts and the blurry ones. If you don't, simply let the thank-yous pile up, one memory at a time. The bell holds the time.
Sylvester. The pope of Constantine's time, little known for certain and wrapped in legend, whose feast closes the calendar year. Today's word.
Your line: the year's last saint. Today, before you sleep, name three things from this year you're glad happened, one out loud. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

1060.title: The saints next door
1060.hook: Pope Francis wrote of holiness in ordinary people nearby
1060.tomorrow: Year three close: the long story is yours
1060.howItsDone: Catholics honor canonized saints on their feast days and also hold, with the Second Vatican Council, that every baptized person is called to holiness; on All Saints' Day the Church celebrates all the saints, including the holy ones no calendar names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sylvester, the pope whose name ends the calendar year. Your line was the year's last saint. Which moment from the year did you say thank you for? Today, the last day of saints across the calendar. Day one thousand sixty.

Since January we've walked the calendar: martyrs and popes, a monk in a boat, a girl with candles in her hair, an archbishop by an open door. Every one of them has a feast day and a statue somewhere. Now look at the woman two doors down who drives her neighbor to chemo every Tuesday. The grandfather who still prays before every meal, even in restaurants. The nurse on nights. None of them has a feast day. Today's question: does holiness need one?
screen: `A YEAR OF FEAST DAYS.` → `THE WOMAN TWO DOORS DOWN.` → `DOES HOLINESS NEED A FEAST?`

segments.voice: Start with how Paul writes his letters. He doesn't address them to a few heroes. He writes to whole congregations, people with jobs and worries and quarrels, and calls them saints. Philippians opens, in the Douay-Rheims, "to all the saints in Christ Jesus." The Greek word is hagioi, the holy ones, set apart for God. In Paul's letters it's what the ordinary baptized are called. Over the centuries the Church came to use the word in a narrower way too: those it formally declares to be in heaven, with a feast day and a place in the calendar. Both senses are still alive in Catholic teaching. The Second Vatican Council spoke of a universal call to holiness, meaning every Christian, not only priests and nuns. And Pope Francis took that up in a letter on holiness called Gaudete et Exsultate, rejoice and be glad. He wrote about the saints next door, his phrase. He pointed to parents raising their children with great love, to men and women working hard to support their families, to the sick, to elderly religious who keep smiling. People living close to us, he wrote, who reflect God's presence. He also warned against the idea that holiness means swooning in mystic rapture. For him, it often looks like small gestures: not gossiping, listening patiently, stopping to say a kind word to someone poor. So the calendar we've walked this year isn't a list of a few superhumans with everybody else watching. It's a family album, and the Church says the album isn't finished.
screen: `PAUL CALLS WHOLE CHURCHES SAINTS.` · `A UNIVERSAL CALL TO HOLINESS.` · `THE SAINTS NEXT DOOR.` · `HOLINESS IN SMALL GESTURES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a holy person you know. Settle, and breathe. Let one face come to mind: someone whose goodness is quiet and steady, who will never be in a stained-glass window. A grandmother, a coworker, a neighbor, a friend in recovery. Stay with their face. Remember one small thing they did that nobody else noticed. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, simply thank them in your heart. Then decide how you'll actually tell them, a text, a call, a note. The bell holds the time.
The saints next door. Pope Francis's phrase for holiness in ordinary people close to us, rooted in Paul calling whole churches saints. Today's word.
Your line: the saint next door. Today, send the message you decided on, a few honest words thanking the person whose face came to you. Day one thousand sixty.

1061.title: Year three close: the long story is yours
1061.hook: from the apostles to now, saints and sinners, and now your chapter
1061.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Church's history alive through the calendar of saints, the readings at Mass and the lives of the saints, and some families keep notes of their own faith story alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the saints next door, Pope Francis's phrase for holiness close by. Your line was the saint next door. Did you send that message? Today, the last day of year three. Day one thousand sixty-one.

The Acts of the Apostles doesn't end the way a book usually ends. Paul is in Rome, under guard in a rented house, and people keep coming to see him. There's no trial verdict, no farewell, no last scene. Luke just stops, with Paul still talking. Some readers have wondered why. This year began right there, at the edge of that unfinished page, and asked: what happened next? Today we look back at the answer, and find out whose turn it is.
screen: `ACTS STOPS MID-STORY.` → `PAUL STILL TALKING IN ROME.` → `WHAT HAPPENED NEXT?`

segments.voice: Here's how Acts ends, in the Douay-Rheims. Paul is preaching the kingdom of God "with all confidence, without prohibition." Then nothing. The story spills off the page. Year three picked it up. First, the first Christians and the Fathers: Peter and Paul in Rome, a fish scratched on a catacomb wall, martyrs and bishops and the great teachers. Second, the councils: bishops arguing out who Christ is, and the words of the creed said at Sunday Mass. Third, the middle ages: monastery bells, bread and books, reformers, builders, a church trying to tame knights. Fourth, reform, mission and revolution: a soldier with a smashed leg reading saints' lives in bed, missionaries crossing oceans, a Church shaken and renewed. Fifth, the modern Church: a parish priest hearing confessions for hours on end, an Oxford scholar following his conscience, councils and popes facing a new world. And then the saints across the calendar, day by day, ending yesterday with the ones next door. This year opened with a line: saints and sinners, both. The Church's history isn't a parade of heroes. It holds martyrs and cowards, reformers and the people who needed reforming, a king's friend killed in his own cathedral. The Church has even asked forgiveness, in public, for sins committed by its own members. And Catholic teaching holds that God kept working through all of it, through weak people as well as strong ones. That's the carry. If Acts ends mid-story, then the generations since have been writing the next line. The story the Church tells about itself is still being written, by people alive now. And whoever is listening has a chapter of their own, whatever they make of that older story.
screen: `WITH ALL CONFIDENCE, WITHOUT PROHIBITION.` · `FATHERS, COUNCILS, MIDDLE AGES.` · `REFORM, MISSION, THE MODERN CHURCH.` · `SAINTS AND SINNERS, BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line of your own chapter. Find a pen and a scrap of paper, or your phone. Settle, and breathe. Let this year pass by: the people you met in these lessons, and the people in your own life. Then ask one question: if someone wrote down this year of mine, what is one true sentence they'd want to include? Not a resolution. Not a speech. One honest line about where you are. Write it. If you pray, you can hold it up to God as part of the longer story. If you don't, just keep it somewhere you'll find it next year. The bell holds the time.
Year three close. The story after Acts, from the first Christians to the saints next door, kept honestly, saints and sinners both, and still being written. Today's word.
Your line: your chapter. Today, put the sentence you wrote somewhere you'll see it, a drawer, a book, a note on your phone, and read it once more before you sleep. Day one thousand sixty-one.
